altyazi.metin: From a distance, wind turbines look
calm. But inside each one, a machine
weighing hundreds of tonnes is at work.
In this video we take a wind turbine
apart, piece by piece.
Our example is the NREL five-megawatt
reference turbine that engineers use in
their calculations: a rotor one hundred
twenty-six metres across, with the hub
ninety metres up.
First, the wind itself.
The Sun does not heat the Earth evenly.
Warm air gets lighter and rises, and
cooler air flows in to replace it.
We call that flow wind.
The power in the wind grows with the
cube of its speed: double the wind
speed, and the power goes up eight
times. This turbine starts turning at
three metres per second and reaches full
power, five megawatts, at eleven point
four.
The blades are shaped like aircraft
wings. They start round at the root,
then taper and twist toward the tip.
Each is sixty-one and a half metres long
and weighs about seventeen and a half
tonnes. Layers of glass fibre are laid
into giant moulds, carbon spar caps
carry the main load, and shear webs tie
the two shells together.
Balsa or foam cores fill the gaps, then
resin bonds everything into a single
piece.
The housing on top of the tower is
called the nacelle; on this turbine it
weighs about two hundred forty tonnes.
The rotor turns at no more than about
twelve revolutions per minute.
That slow rotation passes from the main
shaft into the gearbox.
The gearbox raises the speed
ninety-seven times, so the generator
spins at eleven hundred seventy-four
rpm. A brake disc sits on the fast
shaft, with the power converter,
transformer and cooler at the back and
wind sensors on the roof.
Some turbines have no gearbox at all;
the generator turns directly with the
rotor.
At this size, just moving the blades is
a project of its own.
They ride on special extendable trailers
that stretch to fit the load.
Bridges, bends and junctions are
measured in advance, and sometimes the
whole route is planned from scratch.
On site, a foundation is poured with
hundreds of tonnes of concrete and
anchor bolts are set in place.
Huge crawler cranes stack the tower
sections one by one.
Then the nacelle, and finally the rotor,
made of the hub and blades, are lifted
ninety metres into the air.
On this turbine, the tower alone weighs
about three hundred forty-seven tonnes.
When wind hits a blade, a pressure
difference builds up between its two
faces. This lift force turns the rotor.
The rotation passes through the gearbox
to the generator and becomes
electricity. The power converter matches
the grid frequency, and the transformer
steps up the voltage.
The electricity travels down inside the
tower and flows into the grid.
The turbine is constantly adjusting
itself. When the wind changes direction,
yaw motors turn the nacelle to face it.
Above rated wind speed, the blades
rotate around their own axes; this is
called pitch, and it spills the extra
power. If the wind goes above
twenty-five metres per second, the
blades turn parallel to the wind, the
rotor slows down, and the turbine
protects itself.
No fuel, no smoke; just moving air.
